claim: Alternative polyadenylation yields many mRNA isoforms whose 3' termini occur disproportionately in clusters within 3' untranslated regions.
source: Alternative polyadenylation yields many mRNA isoforms whose 3' termini occur disproportionately in clusters within 3' untranslated regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's own data showing clustering patterns in Figure 1 and by the computational analysis of isoform distributions.

claim: Profiles of poly(A) site usage are regulated by the rate of transcriptional elongation by RNA polymerase II.
source: Previously, we showed that profiles of poly(A) site usage are regulated by the rate of transcriptional elongation by RNA polymerase (Pol) II (Geisberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Pol II derivatives with slow elongation rates confer an upstream-shifted poly(A) profile.
source: Pol II derivatives with slow elongation rates confer an upstream-shifted poly(A) profile, whereas fast Pol II strains confer a downstream-shifted poly(A) profile.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3 comparing slow Pol II mutants to wild-type.

claim: Fast Pol II strains confer a downstream-shifted poly(A) profile.
source: Pol II derivatives with slow elongation rates confer an upstream-shifted poly(A) profile, whereas fast Pol II strains confer a downstream-shifted poly(A) profile.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 comparing fast Pol II mutants to wild-type.

claim: Within yeast isoform clusters, poly(A) profile shifts occur steadily from one isoform to the next across nucleotide distances.
source: Within yeast isoform clusters, these shifts occur steadily from one isoform to the next across nucleotide distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 2B showing continuous changes in mutant/wild-type ratios within clusters.

claim: The shift between clusters is much less pronounced than within clusters, even over large distances.
source: In contrast, the shift between clusters – from the last isoform of one cluster to the first isoform of the next – is much less pronounced, even over large distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 2B showing flat trends between clusters compared to steep trends within clusters.

claim: GC content in a region 13–30 nt downstream from isoform clusters correlates with their sensitivity to Pol II elongation rate.
source: GC content in a region 13–30 nt downstream from isoform clusters correlates with their sensitivity to Pol II elongation rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: In human cells, the upstream shift caused by a slow Pol II mutant occurs continuously at single nucleotide resolution within clusters but not between them.
source: In human cells, the upstream shift caused by a slow Pol II mutant also occurs continuously at single nucleotide resolution within clusters but not between them.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 4B showing continuous changes within clusters and flat trends between clusters in human cells.

claim: Pol II occupancy increases just downstream of poly(A) sites.
source: Pol II occupancy increases just downstream of poly(A) sites, suggesting a linkage between reduced elongation rate and cluster formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Pol II elongation speed affects the nucleotide-level dwell time allowing polyadenylation to occur.
source: These observations suggest that (1) Pol II elongation speed affects the nucleotide-level dwell time allowing polyadenylation to occur
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nucleotide-level correlation between Pol II speed and poly(A) site usage shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Poly(A) site clusters are linked to the local elongation rate and do not arise simply by intrinsically imprecise cleavage and polyadenylation of the RNA substrate.
source: These observations suggest that (1) Pol II elongation speed affects the nucleotide-level dwell time allowing polyadenylation to occur, (2) poly(A) site clusters are linked to the local elongation rate, and hence do not arise simply by intrinsically imprecise cleavage and polyadenylation of the RNA substrate
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Pol II speed affects relative isoform levels within clusters, which would not be expected if clustering were due to intrinsic imprecision.

claim: DNA sequence elements can affect Pol II elongation and poly(A) profiles.
source: These observations suggest that (1) Pol II elongation speed affects the nucleotide-level dwell time allowing polyadenylation to occur, (2) poly(A) site clusters are linked to the local elongation rate, and hence do not arise simply by intrinsically imprecise cleavage and polyadenylation of the RNA substrate, (3) DNA sequence elements can affect Pol II elongation and poly(A) profiles
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation between GC content downstream of clusters and cluster sensitivity to Pol II speed shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cleavage/polyadenylation and Pol II elongation complexes are spatially, and perhaps physically, coupled so that polyadenylation occurs rapidly upon emergence of the nascent RNA from the Pol II elongation complex.
source: These observations suggest that (1) Pol II elongation speed affects the nucleotide-level dwell time allowing polyadenylation to occur, (2) poly(A) site clusters are linked to the local elongation rate, and hence do not arise simply by intrinsically imprecise cleavage and polyadenylation of the RNA substrate, (3) DNA sequence elements can affect Pol II elongation and poly(A) profiles, and (4) the cleavage/polyadenylation and Pol II elongation complexes are spatially, and perhaps physically, coupled so that polyadenylation occurs rapidly upon emergence of the nascent RNA from the Pol II elongation complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nucleotide-level linkage between Pol II position and poly(A) site choice, which suggests tight spatial coupling.

claim: The 3' ends of eukaryotic mRNAs are generated during the process of transcriptional elongation by cleavage of the nascent transcript downstream of the coding region followed by addition of a poly(A) tail.
source: The 3' ends of eukaryotic mRNAs are generated during the process of transcriptional elongation by cleavage of the nascent transcript downstream of the coding region followed by addition of a poly(A) tail (Proudfoot et al., 2002; Tian and Manley, 2013; Tian and Manley, 2017; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Formation of 3' ends is mediated by a multiprotein cleavage/polyadenylation (CpA) complex that performs both steps.
source: Formation of 3' ends is mediated by a multiprotein cleavage/polyadenylation (CpA) complex that performs both steps.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about mRNA 3' end processing.

claim: The poly(A) profile of a typical yeast gene has ~50 mRNA isoforms with 3' endpoints occurring within an 'end zone' of ~200 nt.
source: The poly(A) profile of a typical yeast gene has ~50 mRNA isoforms with 3' endpoints occurring within an 'end zone' of ~200 nt (Ozsolak et al., 2010; Moqtaderi et al., 2013; Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) is a modular entity that is sufficient to determine the poly(A) profile.
source: The 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) is a modular entity that is sufficient to determine the poly(A) profile (Lui et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: mRNA isoforms with neighboring 3' ends can differ dramatically with respect to mRNA stability, structure throughout the 3' UTR, and association with Pab1, the poly(A)-binding protein.
source: Although mRNA isoforms with neighboring 3' ends usually have similar properties, they can differ dramatically with respect to mRNA stability, structure throughout the 3' UTR, and association with Pab1, the poly(A)-binding protein (Geisberg et al., 2014; Moqtaderi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies by the authors.

claim: Polyadenylation rarely occurs within coding regions and introns, even though these are usually much larger than 3' UTRs.
source: Although polyadenylation occurs at numerous sites within the 3' UTR, it rarely occurs within coding regions (Moqtaderi et al., 2013) and introns (Berg et al., 2012), even though these are usually much larger.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Polyadenylation in yeast cells is associated with a degenerate sequence motif consisting of a long AU-rich stretch, followed by short U-rich sequences that flank several A residues immediately downstream of the cleavage site.
source: Polyadenylation in yeast cells is associated with a degenerate sequence motif consisting of a long AU-rich stretch, followed by short U-rich sequences that flank several A residues immediately downstream of the cleavage site (Guo and Sherman, 1996; Moqtaderi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Long AU-rich stretches are important for restricting polyadenylation to 3' UTRs.
source: It has been suggested that long AU-rich stretches, which are not encountered until after coding regions, are important for restricting polyadenylation to 3' UTRs (Lui et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In metazoan mRNAs, an AAUAAA sequence is specifically recognized by the CpA complex.
source: In metazoan mRNAs, an AAUAAA sequence is specifically recognized by the CpA complex (Chan et al., 2014; Schönemann et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), and it contributes significantly to determining where polyadenylation occurs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: AAUAAA contributes significantly to determining where polyadenylation occurs in metazoan mRNAs.
source: In metazoan mRNAs, an AAUAAA sequence is specifically recognized by the CpA complex (Chan et al., 2014; Schönemann et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), and it contributes significantly to determining where polyadenylation occurs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: AAUAAA cannot be the only determinant of poly(A) sites given its high frequency in the transcriptome.
source: However, given its high frequency in the transcriptome, AAUAAA cannot be the only determinant of poly(A) sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that AAUAAA is common but polyadenylation is specific.

claim: The large number of 3' mRNA isoforms for individual genes indicates that the CpA machinery has relatively low sequence specificity.
source: The large number of 3' mRNA isoforms for individual genes indicates that the CpA machinery has relatively low sequence specificity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of many isoforms per gene.

claim: 3' isoform endpoints tend to occur in clusters within the 3' UTR.
source: In addition, as previously noted and shown explicitly here, 3' isoform endpoints tend to occur in clusters within the 3' UTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Clustering of poly(A) sites is usually explained by imprecision of the CpA machinery in the vicinity of a sequence recognition element and/or a preferred cleavage site.
source: Such clustering, which is related to microheterogeneity, is usually explained by imprecision of the CpA machinery in the vicinity of a sequence recognition element (e.g. AAUAAA) and/or a preferred cleavage site.
evidence: This claim represents a commonly held view in the field.

claim: Polyadenylation is intimately connected to the process of transcriptional elongation in vivo.
source: Polyadenylation is intimately connected to the process of transcriptional elongation in vivo (Nag et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Cortazar et al., 2019; Goering et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Transcriptional pausing increases polyadenylation in vitro.
source: Polyadenylation is intimately connected to the process of transcriptional elongation in vivo (Nag et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Cortazar et al., 2019; Goering et al., 2021), and transcriptional pausing increases polyadenylation in vitro (Yonaha and Proudfoot, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: An intact RNA tether between RNA polymerase II and the poly(A) site is required for efficient 3' end processing.
source: An intact RNA tether between RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and the poly(A) site is required for efficient 3' end processing (Bird et al., 2005; Rigo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cleavage of the nascent mRNA leads to polyadenylation and is the key step that initiates transcriptional termination and subsequent export of polyadenylated mRNAs from the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, cleavage of the nascent mRNA not only leads to polyadenylation but is also the key step that initiates the processes of transcriptional termination and subsequent export of polyadenylated mRNAs from the nucleus (Connelly and Manley, 1988; Kim et al., 2004; West et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Each nascent mRNA molecule is cleaved and polyadenylated just once, so the poly(A) profile represents an ensemble of independent events.
source: In general, each nascent mRNA molecule is cleaved and polyadenylated just once, so the poly(A) profile represents an ensemble of independent events.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about mRNA processing.

claim: At some human genes, longer isoforms can be retained in the nuclear matrix and be processed into shorter poly(A) isoforms.
source: However, at some human genes, it has been suggested that longer isoforms can be retained in the nuclear matrix and be processed into shorter poly(A) isoforms (Tang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The poly(A) profiles of most yeast genes are altered in cells expressing Pol II derivatives with altered elongation rates.
source: The poly(A) profiles of most yeast genes are altered in cells expressing Pol II derivatives with altered elongation rates (Geisberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: In all cases of altered Pol II elongation rates, the same poly(A) sites are used but to different extents.
source: In all cases, the same poly(A) sites are used but to different extents.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in the manuscript showing shifts in relative usage rather than appearance of new sites.

claim: Two slow Pol II mutants each cause a 5' shift in poly(A) site use, with the slower mutant giving rise to a greater upstream shift.
source: Two slow Pol II mutants each cause a 5' shift in poly(A) site use, with the slower mutant giving rise to a greater upstream shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 2 comparing 'slow' and 'slower' mutants.

claim: Two fast Pol II mutants cause a 3' shift in preferred poly(A) sites, although the magnitude of this shift is less pronounced, and fewer genes are affected.
source: In contrast, each of two fast Pol II mutants causes a 3' shift in preferred poly(A) sites, although the magnitude of this shift is less pronounced, and fewer genes are affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 3 comparing fast mutants to wild-type.

claim: Altered poly(A) profiles are due to the Pol II elongation rate because strains with reduced Pol II processivity but normal elongation rates have poly(A) profiles indistinguishable from wild-type strains.
source: These altered poly(A) profiles are due to the Pol II elongation rate because strains with reduced Pol II processivity but normal elongation rates have poly(A) profiles indistinguishable from wild-type strains (Geisberg et al., 2020; Yague-Sanz et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Yeast cells undergoing the diauxic response have poly(A) profiles remarkably like those mediated by slow Pol II mutants.
source: Yeast cells undergoing the diauxic response have poly(A) profiles remarkably like those mediated by slow Pol II mutants, indicating the physiological relevance of Pol II elongation rate to poly(A) profiles (Geisberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Transcription slows down in the vicinity of poly(A) sites.
source: Transcription slows down in the vicinity of poly(A) sites, suggesting a functional link between 3' end processing and elongation (Parua et al., 2018; Cortazar et al., 2019; Eaton et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Elongation rate in metazoans affects alternative poly(A) site choice, with slow Pol II mutants favoring the use of more upstream sites.
source: Conversely, elongation rate in metazoans affects alternative poly(A) site choice, with slow Pol II mutants favoring the use of more upstream sites, consistent with a 'window of opportunity' model of poly(A) site choice (Liu et al., 2017; Goering et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Visual inspection suggests that yeast 3' mRNA isoforms are not randomly distributed but rather appear to occur in clusters of closely-spaced poly(A) sites.
source: Within this 'end zone', visual inspection suggests that isoforms are not randomly distributed but rather appear to occur in clusters of closely-spaced poly(A) sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The prevalence of clustered isoform endpoints in each 3' UTR is far higher than that obtained by randomly distributing the same number of major isoforms over the same window.
source: The prevalence of clustered isoform endpoints in each 3' UTR is far higher than that obtained by randomly distributing the same number of major isoforms over the same window (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the randomization analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 3' UTRs containing larger numbers of isoforms give rise to wider clusters and more complex cluster patterns that are exceedingly unlikely to be observed by chance.
source: As expected, 3' UTRs containing larger numbers of isoforms give rise to wider clusters but also to more complex cluster patterns that are exceedingly unlikely to be observed by chance (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Poly(A) site isoforms occur disproportionately in clusters.
source: Thus, poly(A) site isoforms occur disproportionately in clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1.

claim: The Pol II elongation rate has no effect on isoform clustering.
source: The Pol II elongation rate has no effect on isoform clustering (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Within isoform clusters, both the 'slower':wild-type and the 'slow':wild-type ratios continuously decrease from the most ORF-proximal to the most ORF-distal isoforms.
source: Within isoform clusters, both the 'slower':wild-type and the 'slow':wild-type ratios continuously decrease from the most ORF-proximal to the most ORF-distal isoforms; i.e., the most downstream isoform within a cluster typically has the lowest slow:wild-type ratio.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The most downstream isoform within a cluster typically has the lowest slow:wild-type ratio.
source: Within isoform clusters, both the 'slower':wild-type and the 'slow':wild-type ratios continuously decrease from the most ORF-proximal to the most ORF-distal isoforms; i.e., the most downstream isoform within a cluster typically has the lowest slow:wild-type ratio.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Decreases in the slow:wild-type ratios occur continuously at the nucleotide level within clusters.
source: Remarkably, these decreases in the slow:wild-type ratios occur continuously at the nucleotide level (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The intra-cluster slope is steeper in the strain with the 'slower' Pol II derivative as compared to the 'slow' derivative.
source: In addition, the intra-cluster slope is steeper (i.e. the ratio decreases more rapidly) in the strain with the 'slower' Pol II derivative as compared to the 'slow' derivative.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B comparing the two slow mutants.

claim: Both slow:wild-type ratios decrease only very slightly for isoforms from the end of one cluster to the beginning of the next cluster, even over large distances.
source: In contrast, both slow:wild-type ratios decrease only very slightly for isoforms from the end of one cluster to the beginning of the next cluster, even over large distances (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Within a cluster, ORF-distal isoforms typically have the highest fast:wild-type expression ratios, with the overall ratios increasing continuously at the nucleotide level.
source: Within a cluster, ORF-distal isoforms typically have the highest fast:wild-type expression ratios, with the overall ratios increasing continuously at the nucleotide level (specific example shown in Figure 3A, and transcriptome-scale results shown in Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The 'faster' Pol II derivative shows a steeper median slope than the 'fast' derivative.
source: As observed with the 'slow' and 'slower' Pol II derivatives, the 'faster' Pol II derivative shows a steeper median slope than the 'fast' derivative (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The slope of the ratio change is much flatter between clusters for fast Pol II derivatives.
source: As with both slow Pol II derivatives, the slope of the ratio change is much flatter between clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The nucleotide-level linkage between Pol II elongation and polyadenylation is independent of the precise cluster definition used.
source: Again, this effect is independent of the precise cluster definition used (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slow-elongation Pol II derivative with the Rpb1-R749H mutation often confers an upstream shift in the poly(A) profile resembling that observed in yeast slow Pol II mutants, though occurring at fewer genes.
source: This slow-elongation Pol II derivative often confers an upstream shift in the poly(A) profile resembling that observed in yeast slow Pol II mutants, though occurring at fewer genes (Goering et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Within clusters in human cells, the median R749H:wild-type ratio exhibits a continuous, nucleotide-level decrease that resembles the decreases observed with both yeast slow Pol II derivatives.
source: Remarkably, within clusters the median R749H:wild-type ratio exhibits a continuous, nucleotide-level decrease that resembles the decreases observed with both yeast slow Pol II derivatives (an example is shown in Figure 4A, and transcriptome-scale results shown in Figure 4B; compare Figure 4B to Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: In human cells, R749H:wild-type ratios of isoforms from one cluster to the next exhibit much less change.
source: As observed in yeast, R749H:wild-type ratios of isoforms from one cluster to the next exhibit much less change (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The nucleotide-level decrease within clusters observed for R749H:wild-type ratios is independent of both 3' UTR length and the minimal inter-cluster distance used for cluster definition.
source: Importantly, the nucleotide-level decrease within clusters observed for R749H:wild-type ratios is independent of both 3' UTR length and the minimal inter-cluster distance used for cluster definition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For both yeast slow Pol II mutants and at all distances, the mutant:wild-type expression ratio of the downstream isoform is lower than that of the upstream isoform.
source: For both yeast slow Pol II mutants and at all distances, the mutant:wild-type expression ratio of the downstream isoform is lower than that of the upstream isoform; the lower the value, the greater the upstream shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 'slower' Pol II mutant confers a greater upstream shift than the 'slow' Pol II derivative.
source: As expected, the 'slower' Pol II mutant confers a greater upstream shift than the 'slow' Pol II derivative.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The magnitude of the upstream shift increases slightly with distance at isoform spacings between one and five nucleotides, but it is essentially constant at distances greater than five nucleotides.
source: Interestingly, the magnitude of the upstream shift increases slightly with distance at isoform spacings between one and five nucleotides, but it is essentially constant at distances greater than five nucleotides (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In human cells expressing the slow R749H vs. the wild-type α-amanitin resistant Rpb1 derivatives, there are consistently lower slow:wild-type expression ratios at downstream positions relative to upstream positions within clusters.
source: Similar analysis of human cells expressing the slow R749H vs. the wild-type α-amanitin resistant Rpb1 derivatives yields roughly comparable results, with consistently lower slow:wild-type expression ratios at downstream positions relative to upstream positions within clusters (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In both yeast and human cells, the apparent discordance between slow Pol II effects on isoforms within or between clusters largely reflects the greater distance between consecutive isoforms, not the overall distance traveled by Pol II.
source: Thus, in both yeast and human cells, the apparent discordance between slow Pol II effects on isoforms within or between clusters largely reflects the greater distance between consecutive isoforms, not the overall distance traveled by Pol II.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cluster-independent analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In yeast Pol II mutant strains, increased GC content in the region 13–30 bp downstream of a cluster's most ORF-distal isoform is strongly correlated with more steeply declining 'slower':wild-type and 'slow':wild-type isoform utilization and more steeply rising 'fast':wild-type and 'faster':wild-type isoform ratios.
source: However, in yeast Pol II mutant strains, increased GC content in the region 13–30 bp downstream of a cluster's most ORF-distal isoform is strongly correlated with more steeply declining (decreasing 'slower':wild-type Pol II and 'slow':wild-type Pol II isoform utilization) and more steeply rising (increasing 'fast':wild-type and 'faster':wild-type isoform ratios) cluster slopes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 'Slower':wild-type and 'slow':wild-type clusters display excess GC content at +13 to +30 regions when cluster slopes are highly negative and reduced GC content when cluster slopes are positive.
source: 'Slower':wild-type Pol II and 'slow':wild-type Pol II clusters display excess GC content at +13 to +30 regions when cluster slopes are highly negative and reduced GC content when cluster slopes are positive (red and orange bars, respectively; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 'Fast':wild-type and 'faster':wild-type clusters exhibit increased GC content at +13 to +30 when their slopes are highly positive and lower relative GC content as the cluster slopes decrease.
source: Conversely, 'fast':wild-type Pol II and 'faster':wild-type Pol II clusters exhibit increased GC content at +13 to +30 when their slopes are highly positive and lower relative GC content as the cluster slopes decrease (light and dark green bars, respectively; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The contrasting relationships between slow and fast Pol II mutants and GC content downstream of clusters strongly suggest that GC composition at +13 to +30 plays an important role in shaping polyadenylation patterns in clusters by affecting Pol II speed.
source: The contrasting relationships between slow and fast Pol II mutants and GC content downstream of clusters strongly suggest that GC composition at +13 to +30 plays an important role in shaping polyadenylation patterns in clusters by affecting Pol II speed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The distance between the +13 and +30 region and the 3' boundary of an isoform cluster are strikingly similar to the length of the sequence protected by the elongating Pol II machinery.
source: Intriguingly, the distance between the +13 and +30 region and the 3' boundary of an isoform cluster are strikingly similar to the length of the sequence protected by the elongating Pol II machinery (Bernecky et al., 2016; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to structural data cited from Bernecky et al., 2016.

claim: There exists a DNA sequence element that contributes to isoform cluster formation in yeast cells.
source: This observation suggests the existence of a DNA sequence element that contributes to isoform cluster formation in yeast cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GC content correlation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The composite eNETseq profiles around the region of poly(A) sites show decreasing Pol II occupancy just upstream (region between –40 and –1) of poly(A) sites followed by a biphasic increase in Pol II occupancy after the poly(A) site.
source: The composite eNETseq profiles around the region of poly(A) sites show decreasing Pol II occupancy just upstream (region between –40 and –1) of poly(A) sites followed by a biphasic increase in Pol II occupancy after the poly(A) site (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The first increase in Pol II occupancy occurs 10–25 nt downstream of the poly(A) site.
source: The first increase in Pol II occupancy, which presumably corresponds to a slowdown, occurs 10–25 nt downstream of the poly(A) site.
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The poly(A) cleavage site would emerge from the RNA exit channel when Pol II has traveled ~20 nt downstream.
source: Notably, the poly(A) cleavage site would emerge from the RNA exit channel when Pol II has traveled ~20 nt downstream.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural knowledge of Pol II.

claim: The location where the poly(A) cleavage site emerges from the RNA exit channel coincides with the position of the GC-rich region that is linked to isoform clusters in yeast.
source: This location coincides with the position of the GC-rich region that is linked to isoform clusters in yeast.
evidence: This claim is inferred by comparing the eNETseq data to the GC content analysis.

claim: The observations link CpA with a transcriptional slowdown downstream of the poly(A) site.
source: These observations link CpA with a transcriptional slowdown downstream of the poly(A) site.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased Pol II occupancy downstream of poly(A) sites shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The second and stronger increase in Pol II occupancy occurs 30–100 nt downstream of poly(A) sites and appears to be greater in the slow Pol II mutant.
source: The second and stronger increase in Pol II occupancy occurs 30–100 nt downstream of poly(A) sites (Figure 7A) and appears to be greater in the slow Pol II mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The second increase in Pol II occupancy may reflect even slower Pol II speed during the transcriptional termination process, which involves 5'–3' exonucleolytic degradation of the 3' product that remains associated with elongating Pol II after cleavage.
source: It may reflect even slower Pol II speed during the transcriptional termination process, which involves 5'–3' exonucleolytic degradation of the 3' product that remains associated with elongating Pol II after cleavage (Nag et al., 2006; Cortazar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to prior studies on termination.

claim: Pol II occupancy downstream (+30 to +100) of intronic 'decoy' AATAAA sites is roughly comparable to occupancy well upstream (−80 to –100).
source: In contrast to the biphasic increase in Pol II occupancy downstream of poly(A) sites, Pol II occupancy downstream (+30 to +100) of the intronic 'decoy' sites is roughly comparable to occupancy well upstream (−80 to –100).
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Transcription does not slow down at intronic control sites.
source: This observation indicates that transcription does not slow down at intronic control sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Pol II occupancy decreases just upstream (positions –40 to –1) of control sites, as it does with poly(A) sites, although there is high AT content in this region around both control and poly(A) sites.
source: For unknown reasons, Pol II occupancy decreases just upstream (positions –40 to –1) of control sites, as it does with poly(A) sites, although we note that there is high AT content in this region around both control and poly(A) sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the eNETseq data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Pol II occupancy around poly(A) sites in yeast cells exhibits a remarkably similar pattern to that in mammalian cells.
source: Importantly, Pol II occupancy around poly(A) sites in yeast cells exhibits a remarkably similar pattern (Harlen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Yeast Pol II occupancy dips just upstream of poly(A) sites and exhibits a marked increase downstream of them.
source: As in mammalian cells, yeast Pol II occupancy dips just upstream of poly(A) sites and exhibits a marked increase downstream of them (Harlen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The link between recognition and/or processing by the CpA machinery and Pol II slowdown downstream of poly(A) sites appears to be an evolutionarily conserved feature in eukaryotes.
source: Thus, the link between recognition and/or processing by the CpA machinery and Pol II slowdown downstream of poly(A) sites appears to be an evolutionarily conserved feature in eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of patterns in yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: Both slow and fast Pol II derivatives cause poly(A) shifts within isoform clusters that are continuous at the nucleotide level.

evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The nucleotide-level continuity of poly(A) shifts strongly suggests a time dependence in which there is a limited opportunity for poly(A) site cleavage to occur at a given site in the RNA before Pol II continues its journey downstream.
source: This observation strongly suggests a time dependence in which there is a limited opportunity for poly(A) site cleavage to occur at a given site in the RNA before Pol II continues its journey downstream.

claim: Faster Pol II would have a shorter window of opportunity, leading to reduced cleavage at a given site.

source: In general, every mRNA molecule that is cleaved and polyadenylated at a given site can no longer be polyadenylated at any site further downstream.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about mRNA processing.

claim: On a population level, higher polyadenylation frequency at upstream sites means reduced use of downstream poly(A) sites, and lower polyadenylation frequency means increased use of downstream sites.
source: Thus, on a population level, higher polyadenylation frequency at upstream sites means reduced use of downstream poly(A) sites, and lower polyadenylation frequency means increased use of downstream sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the logic of mRNA processing.

claim: An effect of Pol II elongation speed on cleavage at a given polyadenylation site influences the use of downstream poly(A) sites.
source: An effect of Pol II elongation speed on cleavage at a given polyadenylation site therefore influences the use of downstream poly(A) sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the logic of mRNA processing and the data.

claim: The conserved relationship between Pol II speed and poly(A) site choice within clusters suggests that Pol II elongation and polyadenylation are mechanistically linked at the nucleotide level.
source: The conserved relationship between Pol II speed and poly(A) site choice within clusters suggests that Pol II elongation and polyadenylation are mechanistically linked at the nucleotide level.

claim: Once Pol II has traversed the region, the CpA machinery does not go back to the most upstream site but instead tracks with elongating Pol II and uses sites further downstream within the same cluster.
source: Once Pol II has traversed the region, the CpA machinery does not go back to the most upstream site but instead tracks with elongating Pol II (Licatalosi et al., 2002; Ahn et al., 2004; Glover-Cutter et al., 2008) and uses sites further downstream within the same cluster.

claim: If the CpA machinery misses earlier opportunities to act, downstream positions are available to be used as polyadenylation sites.
source: Conversely, if the CpA machinery misses earlier opportunities to act, downstream positions are available to be used as polyadenylation sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the logic of the mechanism.

source: The nucleotide-level coupling of Pol II elongation to poly(A) site choice strongly suggests that co-transcriptional cleavage of the nascent mRNA can, and often does, occur soon after RNA exits the Pol II elongation complex and becomes accessible to the CpA complex.

claim: The region of newly extruded pre-mRNA is still in proximity to the elongating Pol II complex, but just far enough away to allow for efficient binding of the CpA machinery and cleavage of the nascent transcript.
